title: Site Dust Suppression for Air Quality
osha_standards: OSH Act Section 5(a)(1) General Duty Clause
summary: Construction sites can create dust from disturbed soil that harms air quality and worker health. This talk covers common ways to control dust and the limits of each method.
talking_points: Dust from disturbed soil adds fine particles (PM2.5 and PM10) to the air. These particles can contribute to respiratory health problems and create unpleasant working conditions.
Earthmoving, especially hauling cut and fill material, is the major source of dust. Traffic and general disturbance also add to it.
Disturb only small areas at a time. Less exposed soil means less dust.
Sprinkle the ground with water until it is moist, especially on haul roads and traffic routes. Water needs frequent reapplication.
Too much water can run off the site or lead to vehicles tracking mud onto public roads.
Other controls include mulch, vegetative cover, wind breaks, stone on roads and entrances, and tillage.
Chemical dust suppressants should follow the manufacturer's specifications. Misuse can create hazardous working conditions, pollute water, and present a health risk.
Water and chemical controls need more monitoring than structural or vegetative controls.

This talk covers soil dust from earthmoving and traffic. It is not a silica or respirable-dust exposure talk. If work creates dust from cutting, grinding, or drilling concrete or masonry, OSHA's silica standard (29 CFR 1926.1153) applies. State or local requirements may also apply.
site_hazards_to_check: Large areas of bare, dry soil exposed to wind
Haul roads and traffic routes with no dust control
Dust blowing off site or toward neighbors and waterbodies
Mud tracked onto public roads or runoff from over-watering
Chemical dust suppressant used without manufacturer directions
discussion_questions: Where is the most dust coming from on our site today?
What dust control are we using, and how often does it need to be redone?
How can we sequence the work to expose less soil at a time?

attribution.notice: Adapted from EPA's Stormwater Best Management Practice fact sheet, Dust Control (EPA-832-F-21-028R). Reproduced with attribution for jobsite safety training; not an endorsement by EPA. EPA notes that state or local requirements may apply.

flags: Verified facts against the EPA fact sheet: PM2.5/PM10, earthmoving as major source, small disturbed areas, sprinkling and reapplication, over-watering runoff/tracking, other controls, manufacturer specs, monitoring. Fixed one overstatement: 'must follow' manufacturer specs changed to 'should' (source says 'should').

Decision: acceptable with non-blocking flags, consistent with EPA stormwater talks 177/180. Dust from disturbed soil is a legitimate site air-quality and worker-comfort/health topic and the controls are actionable for crews. Weak spots: mapping is General Duty Clause only, source is environmental (stormwater BMP), and it gives no worker exposure limits or respirator guidance. Added a point clarifying it is not a silica talk (1926.1153) and that state/local rules may apply.
